clue.text: Marches, for example, heard? Females in charge

indicators.note: heard asks the solver to say the phrase from the first part out loud and catch a different spelling

parts.note: the March sisters of Little Women are a quartet of girls, a group of four women

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about border marches, then a remark about women running things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Marches' looks like the Welsh border country or protest walks; it is the family name of the four sisters in Louisa May Alcott's Little Women.
explanation.definitionFit: A forewoman is a female supervisor of workers, so the plural names women who are in charge.

indicators.note: within means the I is placed inside the word for a crossing-place

parts.note: a ford is a shallow place where a river can be crossed

explanation.surface: Someone discovers a place to cross the water inside an inlet.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiord, or fjord, is a long narrow sea inlet between cliffs.

definitions.meaning: someone wanting sweeping change
in maths, a root sign expression, which is often an irrational number such as the square root of two

explanation.surface: A political hothead who is often unreasonable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'irrational' looks like unreasonable; in mathematics, a radical such as the square root of 2 is often an irrational number.
explanation.definitionFit: An extremist seeking root-and-branch change, and a root expression in algebra, share the name.

clue.text: Doorstep support for party organizer in fund-raising

indicators.note: in a down clue, a support sits beneath, so the first piece goes below the organizer

parts.note: a whip keeps a political party's members in line
a doorstep is a very thick slice of bread, and a round is a slice or sandwich

explanation.surface: A doorstep canvasser supports the party organiser at a fund-raising drive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doorstep' looks like canvassing; it is British slang for a thick slice of bread, which is also called a round. A whip is the MP who enforces party discipline.
explanation.definitionFit: A whip-round is an informal collection of money among a group, a small fund-raising.

definitions.meaning: a crime or wrongdoing
read whimsically as a group made up of men, a men-only faction

explanation.surface: A complaint caused by a raucous bachelor party.
explanation.walkthrough: A stag party is a British pre-wedding night out for the groom and his male friends; read literally, it is a faction of males.
explanation.definitionFit: Malefaction is an evil deed, and split in two it describes a band of men.

definitions.meaning: slang for taking something quickly
to squeeze between finger and thumb

explanation.surface: Two words for taking or squeezing.
explanation.definitionFit: To nip can mean to dash off with something, or to squeeze sharply.

indicators.note: about means the word for paired goes around the Roman numeral

parts.note: paired things are dual, coming in twos
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: A question about rubber boots, which do come in pairs, numbering about a hundred.
explanation.walkthrough: Wellingtons look like rubber boots, which suits 'Paired'; the question mark points to the Duke of Wellington, so 'like Wellingtons' means belonging to a duke.
explanation.definitionFit: The Duke of Wellington held a dukedom, and ducal is the adjective for things relating to dukes.

definitions.meaning: the famous horse race run at Epsom
the English Midlands city lying between those two

explanation.surface: A race between two English cities.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a contest between two cities; the second definition is a city located between them, Derby in the East Midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: The Epsom flat race is named after an earl, and the East Midlands city lies roughly midway between those two cities.

parts.note: a cell is a small enclosed room or cubicle

indicators.note: leader means only the opening letter of the word team is used

explanation.surface: A sportsman in a changing cubicle happens to be the team captain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'team-leader' looks like a captain; split it, and 'leader' takes the first letter of 'team'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cellist plays the cello, a musical performer.

clue.text: Modern fashions treat lady in a certain way …

indicators.note: fashions is a verb here, meaning shapes the following letters into a new form

explanation.surface: Contemporary trends treat a woman in a particular way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fashions' looks like a noun for trends; it is the verb, rearranging TREAT LADY. The ellipsis leads on to the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Latter-day means of recent times, a present-day version of something older.

parts.note: something that is not new is old
a bill is a charge for goods or services

explanation.surface: The police are accused of bringing a charge without fresh evidence.
explanation.walkthrough: THE OLD BILL is British slang for the police.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang term for the police force, as heard in London speech and TV dramas.

clue.text: Separate rent in old woman's garment

parts.note: to separate two things is to part them
to let a property is to rent it out

explanation.surface: Advice to split the rent, oddly sitting inside a phrase about an old lady's clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rent' looks like a tear in the garment; here it is the verb, as in letting a flat. A partlet was a sixteenth-century covering for a woman's neck and shoulders.
explanation.definitionFit: A historical collar or ruffled neck covering worn by women in Tudor times.

indicators.note: section in says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Stage instructions to include a corner section of the set.
explanation.definitionFit: On a stage, the decor is the set dressing and backdrops, the visual setting of a play.

definitions.meaning: a single played at 45 revolutions per minute
four tens plus five as a figure
the Jacobite rebellion of 1745 led by Bonnie Prince Charlie

explanation.surface: A record number of people rising up.
explanation.walkthrough: Three definitions: a 7-inch single spinning at that speed, the number itself, and 'the Forty-Five', the 1745 Jacobite uprising in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A vinyl single, a figure, and the name for the 1745 Jacobite rebellion all share this name.

indicators.note: in a setting means the short skirts are mounted inside the word for contemporary, like a jewel in its setting

parts.note: something contemporary is recent
minis are very short skirts

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: memories of short skirts in a modern scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'skirts' looks like a verb, as in avoids; it is the plural noun, MINIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Something reminiscent brings back memories, calling the past to mind.

clue.text: It sounds unexceptional, and can be boring

indicators.note: It sounds tells the solver the answer is pronounced like another word

parts.note: with no exception means every one, or all

explanation.surface: A remark that something sounds ordinary and possibly dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unexceptional' looks like 'ordinary', and 'boring' like 'dull'; read instead 'without exception' and 'drilling holes'.
explanation.definitionFit: An awl is a pointed tool for piercing holes in leather or wood, so it bores.

clue.text: Judge removing one right from confused barristers

indicators.note: confused means the remaining letters are jumbled
removing means one letter is taken out of the word barristers before it is rearranged

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right; only one of the three is removed

explanation.surface: A judge leaves out one correct point from a muddled band of lawyers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'removing' takes one R from BARRISTERS, and 'confused' rearranges what remains, BAISTERRS.
explanation.definitionFit: An arbitress is a woman who arbitrates, deciding disputes between parties.

clue.text: Lacking convictions so not sent to prison

definitions.meaning: having no firm beliefs or allegiance
not consigned to jail by a court

explanation.surface: A person cleared by the courts is therefore not jailed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'convictions' pretends to be the legal sense; the first definition is about beliefs, and the second is the legal one.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone undecided holds no fixed opinions, and a defendant never committed for trial or custody stays free.

clue.text: David, for example, is artist of top quality

parts.note: RA is a Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts
the elite are the very best

explanation.surface: Michelangelo's David, say, is the work of a first-class artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'David' suggests Michelangelo's statue; it is King David of Israel.
explanation.definitionFit: King David was a member of the ancient Hebrew people, so he is an example.

clue.text: Family's supporter had success in stud, we hear

indicators.note: we hear means the phrase is pronounced like the answer though spelt differently

parts.note: a stud farm that bred a winner had a successful racehorse born there

explanation.surface: A family's provider has done well breeding horses at a stud farm.
explanation.walkthrough: A stud is a farm where horses are bred.
explanation.definitionFit: The earner whose wages keep a household fed is its main financial provider.

indicators.note: included means a letter is placed inside the name of the symphony

parts.note: the Eroica is Beethoven's Third Symphony

indicators.note: initially says the opening letter of toccata is taken

explanation.surface: A symphony with a toccata included makes for thrilling music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rousing' suggests stirring music; here it means sexually arousing.
explanation.definitionFit: Erotica is literature or art meant to arouse sexual desire.

definitions.meaning: a cry to attract someone's attention, as in ahoy
a small coastal sailing vessel carrying cargo

explanation.surface: Someone calling out to warn a merchant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trader' looks like a merchant; it is a trading boat, a hoy being a small coaster.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an old call to hail someone and also the name of a small cargo-carrying coastal boat.

parts.note: read as food served to people up in the sky, a lofty afternoon meal of tea and cooked dishes

explanation.surface: A question about the price of an airline ticket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fare' looks like a ticket price; it is food, and 'air passengers' are people high up. In Britain this is an early evening meal with tea.
explanation.definitionFit: High tea is a substantial early evening meal, and here punningly food eaten at altitude.

definitions.meaning: the Bible says Saul hath slain his ..., and David his ten ...
used loosely for a huge but uncounted crowd

explanation.surface: Saul's victims, spoken of in figures of speech.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half quotes 1 Samuel 18:7; the second reads the plural as loose talk for 'lots'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bible credits Saul with slaying great multitudes, and people casually use the word for any large number.

parts.note: read as a small stroke placed at the extremities of a printed letter, helping form the character

explanation.surface: A remark that something builds a strong personality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'character-forming' suggests moral training; a character here is a letter of type, and the stroke sits at its ends.
explanation.definitionFit: A serif is the fine cross-line finishing a stroke of a printed letter.

clue.text: Trouble for plant as work unit has to return

parts.note: the erg is the unit of work in the old centimetre-gram-second system

indicators.note: return says the little word to is turned backwards

explanation.surface: A problem in a factory because a unit of workers must come back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' looks like a factory; it is a living plant, and ergot is a fungal disease of cereals such as rye.
explanation.definitionFit: Ergot is a fungus that infects rye and other grasses, a blight on crops.

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law

indicators.note: end of means the last letter of the word chocolate is taken

explanation.surface: Someone has the wrong end of a chocolate cake.
explanation.definitionFit: A torte is a rich, often layered, Central European cake.

clue.text: Short poem depicting last 'of the farm animals

indicators.note: last means the final letter of the word that follows is taken

parts.note: a pig is a farmyard animal
a ram is a male sheep, also kept on farms

explanation.surface: A brief poem portraying the last of the animals on a farm.
explanation.definitionFit: An epigram is a brief, witty verse or saying.

definitions.meaning: to staff a post with troops
in chess, a castle or rook is one of the pieces

explanation.surface: Supplying troops to garrison a castle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'castle' looks like a fortress to garrison; it is the chess piece, and chess pieces are called men.
explanation.definitionFit: To man a post is to staff it, and any chess piece is a man.

clue.text: Person who has to expel Eton's head boy

indicators.note: head means the first letter of the word Eton is taken

parts.note: Victor is a boy's name

explanation.surface: A headmaster forced to throw out Eton's head boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head boy' looks like a school title; 'head' goes with Eton's, and 'boy' is a name. Eton is a famous English public school.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who turns tenants out of a property is a person whose job is to throw them out.

definitions.meaning: a pole or rod carried for support
the teachers and workers in a school

explanation.surface: A cane used in schools.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests corporal punishment; the second definition is the people who work there.
explanation.definitionFit: A walking pole is one sense, and the workforce of a school or office is another.

clue.text: I'll cite insane pronouncement locating this building

definitions.text: I'll cite insane pronouncement locating this building

parts.words: I'll cite insane pronouncement locating this building
parts.note: said aloud, I'll cite in Seine gives Ile de la Cite in the Seine, the Paris island where this famous cathedral stands

explanation.surface: A madman announces that he will quote something about where a building is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'insane' looks like madness; spoken, 'I'll cite insane' is the Île de la Cité in the Seine, the Paris island on which the Gothic cathedral stands.
explanation.definitionFit: The great Gothic cathedral of Paris stands on the island in the Seine.
